content: 1. The practice of law enforcement using the possession of condoms as evidence of sex work and grounds for arrest should be abolished. This approach is counterproductive and perpetuates stigma and discrimination. 2. Countries should strive to achieve legal recognition for transgender and gender-diverse individuals, ensuring their rights and dignity are upheld. 3. Policymakers are encouraged to review and revise consent policies to reduce age-related barriers to accessing HIV, STI, and viral hepatitis services. This would empower healthcare providers to act in the best interests of adolescents. 4. Governments should implement and enforce anti-discrimination and protective laws based on human rights standards to eliminate stigma, discrimination, and violence against key populations. 5. Collaboration between policymakers, parliamentarians, public health leaders, and civil society organizations, including those led by key populations, is essential to monitor stigma, address discrimination, and reform punitive legal and social norms. 6. Health services must be accessible, acceptable, and equitable for key populations, adhering to principles of medical ethics, non-discrimination, and the right to health. 7. Countries should develop non-custodial alternatives to incarceration for drug users, sex workers, and individuals engaging in same-sex activities, as outlined in the 2014 WHO guidelines. 8. Compulsory or involuntary treatment, including for drug dependence, conversion therapy, or rehabilitation of sex workers, violates human rights and medical ethics principles. Such practices should be banned. 9. Healthcare workers should receive ongoing training and sensitization to provide non-discriminatory, confidential, and rights-based services to adults and adolescents from key populations. 10. Safe spaces should be established within healthcare services to protect individuals from stigma and discrimination. These spaces should allow adolescents to express their concerns freely and receive patient, understanding, and non-judgmental care. 11. Key population-led organizations should be integral partners in designing, planning, implementing, and evaluating health services to ensure community empowerment. 12. Programs should include interventions to enhance community empowerment among key populations, such as legal literacy and access to legal services, enabling individuals to understand their rights and seek justice when needed. 13. Violence against key populations must be prevented and addressed in partnership with key population-led organizations. Mechanisms should be established to monitor, report, and provide redress for such violence. 14. Health and support services should be available to all individuals from key populations who experience violence, with timely access to comprehensive post-rape care for survivors of sexual violence. 15. Law enforcement officials and healthcare providers must be trained to recognize and uphold the human rights of key populations. They should be held accountable for any violations, including acts of violence. 16. All individuals who inject drugs should have access to sterile injecting equipment through needle and syringe programs (NSPs). These programs should also provide low dead-space syringes and information on their benefits. 17. Opioid agonist maintenance therapy (OAMT) should be offered to all opioid-dependent individuals, including those in prisons and closed settings, in line with WHO guidelines. 18. Naloxone should be made available to individuals likely to witness an opioid overdose, along with training on its use for emergency overdose management. 19. The consistent and correct use of condoms, along with adequate supplies of condom-compatible lubricants, is strongly recommended to prevent the sexual transmission of HIV, viral hepatitis, and STIs. 20. Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) containing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate should be offered as an additional prevention option for individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection. 21. The dapivirine vaginal ring may be offered as an additional prevention choice for cisgender women at substantial risk of HIV infection, as part of combination prevention approaches. 22. Long-acting injectable cabotegravir may be offered as an additional prevention option for individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection, as part of combination prevention approaches. 23. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) should be made available on a voluntary basis to all eligible individuals from key populations after potential exposure to HIV. 24. For women who have been raped, a package of PEP, emergency contraception, and presumptive treatment for STIs is recommended. 25. HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) tests should be offered at least once and as early as possible during pregnancy, ideally at the first antenatal care visit. 26. Pregnant individuals with high HBV DNA levels should receive tenofovir prophylaxis from the 28th week of pregnancy until at least birth, in addition to the three-dose hepatitis B vaccination for all infants. 27. In settings where antenatal HBV DNA testing is unavailable, hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) testing can be used as an alternative to determine eligibility for tenofovir prophylaxis. 28. Addressing chemsex requires a comprehensive, non-judgmental, and person-centered approach, integrating sexual and reproductive health, mental health, and harm reduction services. 29. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) can be used as the first test in HIV testing strategies during antenatal care, with additional HBsAg testing when dual testing is performed. 30. Programs should offer rapid hepatitis B vaccination regimens to individuals who inject drugs, particularly in high-risk settings.
